drivingQuestion: What does the mishna's 'son' clause teach?
outcomeNote: The clause excludes reading 'son' as any offspring

segments.he: גְּמָ׳ הַאי מַאי לְמֵימְרָא? מִשּׁוּם סֵיפָא: בַּת, טוּמְטוּם וְאַנְדְּרוֹגִינוֹס — אֵינוֹ נָזִיר. פְּשִׁיטָא! מַהוּ דְּתֵימָא: ״לִכְשֶׁאֶבָּנֶה״ הוּא דְּקָאָמַר, קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן דְּלָא.
segments.en: «GEMARA:» With regard to the statement of the mishna that one who vowed to be a nazirite when a son is born to him is a nazirite when his son is born, the Gemara asks: «What» is the purpose «of stating this» ruling? Of course he is a nazirite. The Gemara answers: This halakha is stated «due to the latter clause» of that mishna, which states that if «a daughter, a tumtum, or a hermaphrodite» are born to him, «he is not a nazirite.» The Gemara questions this, too: «Isn’t» that «obvious,» since he specified a son? The Gemara answers: It is necessary «lest you say» he did not literally mean a son, but rather «he meant to say: When I will be built up» by means of any child, including the types listed. The mishna therefore «teaches us that» this is «not» the case.

moves.summary: Why state the obvious first clause?
moves.about: that one who vowed on a son is a nazirite when a son is born is obvious

moves.summary: For the sake of the latter clause

moves.summary: The latter clause is also obvious

moves.summary: Lest one read 'son' as 'being built up' by any child
moves.about: one might think 'son' meant 'when I am built up' by any child; the mishna teaches otherwise
